blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Sort taxes into direct and indirect, and by the share of income each takes: progressive, regressive, proportional.

blocks.heading: Direct and indirect
blocks.text: Direct taxes fall on income or profit and are paid over by the taxed party itself: income tax withheld from wages at Oshakati Textiles, company tax on Marula Foods' profits. Indirect taxes fall on spending and are collected by traders: value-added tax added to a bill in a Gobabis shop, excise duty on fuel in Germany, each collected from buyers and remitted. What settles the sorting is what the charge is levied on and who hands it over.

blocks.heading: By the share of income
blocks.text: A progressive tax takes a rising share of income as income rises; a regressive tax takes a larger share of a low income than of a high one; a proportional tax takes the same share of every income. The share of income, not the amount paid, is what the classification turns on.

blocks.heading: The shares worked out
blocks.text: Work invented figures through: a worker paying N$1 500 of income tax on a N$10 000 wage pays 15 per cent of it, a manager paying N$6 000 on N$30 000 pays 20 per cent - the share rises with income, so the income tax is progressive. Value-added tax at a flat 15 per cent takes the same N$15 from a N$100 basket whatever the buyer earns, but a poorer household spends a larger part of its income on such baskets, so the tax takes a larger share of that household's income - regressive in effect. A proportional tax sits between the two. A flat income tax of 20 per cent takes N$2 000 from a N$10 000 income and N$6 000 from a N$30 000 income: the higher earner pays three times as much money, but the share of income is the same 20 per cent at both levels, so the tax is proportional, not progressive. A common slip is to call a tax progressive because richer people pay more money; the test is the share of income, not the amount. Estonia is one country that charges a single flat rate of income tax on most personal income, and a company tax charged at one rate on all profits works proportionally on profit.

blocks.heading: A consequence is not a cause
blocks.text: After a tax rises, some learners write the effects that follow as though they produced the change. The tax change is the cause; what follows - lower disposable income, dearer goods, changed buying - is its consequence. To check, ask which way the events run.

blocks.heading: Interest rates are not taxes
blocks.text: Asked about a tax measure, some learners reach for the interest rate. An interest rate is the price paid for borrowing money; a tax is a compulsory levy on income or spending. To tell them apart, ask who sets the charge and what it falls on.
